topic: How Do Icebergs Float If They Weigh Millions of Tons
angle: A massive mountain of solid ice weighing millions of tons floats effortlessly on liquid water, defying what heavy objects should naturally do.
why: Massive high-performing explainers like Veritasium and Zack D. Films prove that counterintuitive physics principles pull tens of millions of views. This question is irresistible because it turns an everyday phenomenon into a baffling engineering and physical paradox that everyone sees but nobody truly stops to calculate.
facts: Icebergs are massive chunks of freshwater ice that break off glaciers and float in saltwater oceans.
Water is one of the only substances on Earth that expands when it freezes, making solid ice less dense than liquid water.
Because ice is about 9% less dense than water, it floats rather than sinking to the bottom.
An iceberg floats with only about 10% of its mass visible above the ocean surface.
The remaining 90% of the iceberg's massive weight is completely hidden underwater, which inspired the phrase 'tip of the iceberg'.
A medium-sized iceberg can weigh around 100,000 to 200,000 metric tons.
Despite weighing hundreds of thousands of tons, the buoyant force exerted by the displaced seawater pushes upward with equal strength.
Seawater is actually saltier and denser than the freshwater ice of the iceberg, which helps increase its buoyancy slightly compared to freshwater lakes.
As an iceberg melts, its center of gravity shifts, causing the massive structure to violently roll over or flip completely upside down in the ocean.
The displacement principle governing icebergs was first mathematically formulated by the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes around 250 BC.
